sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Montagu Declaration (August 1917)**: Declared the objective of British policy as the gradual introduction of **responsible government** in India.
• **Introduction of Dyarchy**: Divided provincial subjects into **Transferred** (administered by Governor with ministers responsible to Legislative Council) and **Reserved** (administered by Governor with executive council without responsibility).
• **Bicameralism at the Centre**: Replaced the Indian Legislative Council with a bicameral legislature consisting of the **Council of State** (Upper House) and the **Central Legislative Assembly** (Lower House).
• **Key Metric / Factor**: Franchise was extended, granting voting rights to about **10% of the population** based on property, tax, or education criteria.

items.definition: A system of dual governance introduced in provinces where provincial subjects were divided into Reserved and Transferred categories.
The Upper House created under the 1919 Act with a tenure of 5 years, having a restricted franchise and male-dominated elite membership.
The Lower House created under the 1919 Act with a tenure of 3 years, comprising elected and nominated members.
A new office created in London to take over some of the functions previously performed by the Secretary of State for India.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Governor's Provinces**: Dyarchy was implemented across major British provinces including Bengal, Madras, Bombay, United Provinces, Punjab, Bihar & Orissa, Central Provinces, and Assam.
• **Driving Advantages**: Decentralization of administrative authority and preparation of regional political leadership through local self-government bodies.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Severe financial control of Reserved subjects by the Governor, lack of real executive accountability, and communal representation extension.
• **Policy Interventions**: Demands for revision led to the appointment of the **Muddiman Committee (1924)** and subsequently the **Simon Commission (1927)**.

items.title: Mnemonic for Reserved Subjects
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "FLIP-R" (Finance, Land Revenue, Irrigation, Police, Reserved)
• **Decoded Meaning**: Quick checklist to identify key Reserved subjects under provincial Dyarchy.
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly eliminates incorrect options when UPSC mixes up Transferred and Reserved portfolios.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: 1919 Act brought **Bicameralism** and **Direct Elections** at the **Centre**, while introducing **Dyarchy** at the **Provinces**.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that Dyarchy was introduced at the Centre by the Government of India Act 1919. This is false; Dyarchy was introduced in the **Provinces**, while it was introduced at the Centre later by the Government of India Act 1935.

Mains Value Addition: In GS-2 answers regarding constitutional evolution, analyze the 1919 Act through the lens of 'too little, too late'—how it failed to satisfy nationalist aspirations, leading directly to the Non-Cooperation Movement.

keyTakeaways: The Government of India Act 1919 formally introduced the concept of responsible government and direct elections in India.
It established provincial dyarchy, dividing subjects into Reserved and Transferred, which proved largely unworkable due to executive overreach.
It laid the institutional bedrock for federalism by establishing a bicameral legislature at the central level.
